title: Moral Hazard in Multi-Agent Language Models

1.1 Positioning Relative to Cooperative Games


The game complements standard Prisoner’s Dilemma, public-goods, and sequential social-dilemma evaluations (Axelrod & Hamilton, 1981; Fehr & Gächter, 2000; Leibo et al., 2017). Unlike settings where the cooperative action directly enters shared payoff, our task separates private information acquisition, public communication, and another agent’s use of that information. Table 1 summarizes this distinction; Appendix A provides the broader literature discussion.

Table 1: Construct-level comparison with common cooperative-game paradigms. These paradigms are complementary evaluation targets, not interchangeable measures.


Figure 1: Schematic of one successful Dialogue Moral Hazard Game episode. Agents first face a private choice between preserving local reward and paying a query cost. A query reveals information about another agent’s case, which can be posted as an anonymous warning note and used to make the team-beneficial final choice.

2.2 Construct and Theory-Facing Validity


The decomposed outcomes identify where autonomous play succeeds or fails, but they do not by themselves establish that behavior responds to the intended incentives. We therefore use two complementary experiments. Autonomous payoff sweeps retain the complete query–warning–decision pipeline while varying query cost, team reward, or group size, testing whether end-to-end behavior responds to the payoff contract. A private-share incentive-isolation experiment then scripts all partner behavior while independently varying query cost and the focal agent’s share of team output, testing the Holmström-style private incentive comparison without downstream reasoning, communication, or formatting failures.


Figure 2: GPT-5.6 Sol sensitivity to query cost (A), team reward (B), and group size (C). Lines show percentage means and translucent bands show ±1\pm 1 standard deviation across three repeated API sampling replicates of 15 episodes each. The primary setting is k=0.10k=0.10, wT=0.50w_{T}=0.50, and n=2n=2; parameters not shown on a panel’s x-axis are held fixed at these values.


Figure 2 first tests the full autonomous pipeline. Under the primary weights, the all-query route has value wF+wT−kw_{F}+w_{T}-k and the local route has value wLw_{L}, giving predicted indifference points of k∗=wF+wT−wL=0.30k^{*}=w_{F}+w_{T}-w_{L}=0.30 for query cost and wT∗=wL+k−wF=0.30w_{T}^{*}=w_{L}+k-w_{F}=0.30 for team reward. The query-cost sweep resolves the expected transition: as kk rises from 0.150.15 to 0.400.40, query rate falls from 98.9±1.9%98.9\pm 1.9\% to 4.4±1.9%4.4\pm 1.9\%, team success falls from 97.8±3.8%97.8\pm 3.8\% to 0.0±0.0%0.0\pm 0.0\%, and local-reward preservation rises from 1.1±1.9%1.1\pm 1.9\% to 94.4±1.9%94.4\pm 1.9\%. At the predicted boundary k=0.30k=0.30, the model mixes between routes (70.0±8.8%70.0\pm 8.8\% query) rather than remaining at either ceiling.


The team-reward sweep supplies the complementary intervention. Query rate rises from 0.0±0.0%0.0\pm 0.0\% at wT=0.20w_{T}=0.20 to 66.7±14.5%66.7\pm 14.5\% at the predicted boundary wT=0.30w_{T}=0.30, 90.0±3.3%90.0\pm 3.3\% at wT=0.40w_{T}=0.40, and 100.0±0.0%100.0\pm 0.0\% at wT=0.50w_{T}=0.50. Cost and team reward thus move the query decision in opposite predicted directions while the rest of the autonomous pipeline is held fixed.


The group-size sweep qualifies that evidence rather than extending it into a universal theory result. From n=6n=6 through n=9n=9, query rate remains between 97.0%97.0\% and 99.0%99.0\%, while team success varies non-monotonically from 82.2%82.2\% to 93.3%93.3\%. This ceiling-regime experiment shows that the ring protocol remains executable at larger group sizes, but it does not validate a monotonic larger-team shirking prediction.


Private-share incentive isolation.


Because the autonomous sweeps leave every link in the query–warning–decision chain active, they cannot isolate incentives from downstream capabilities. We therefore script partner behavior and define the focal agent’s private payoff as

where αi\alpha_{i} is the focal agent’s private share of the fixed team-success value. Shares sum to one, so changing αi\alpha_{i} redistributes private credit without changing the social score. Scripted partners ensure that Fi=1F_{i}=1 under either first-step action, query produces T=1T=1, and local produces T=0T=0. The focal comparison therefore reduces exactly to




mi≡Ui​(query)−Ui​(local)=n​αi​wT−wL−k.m_{i}\equiv U_{i}(\textsc{query})-U_{i}(\textsc{local})=n\alpha_{i}w_{T}-w_{L}-k.

(4)


With n=2n=2, wL=0.35w_{L}=0.35, and wT=0.50w_{T}=0.50, the predicted private indifference boundary is




α∗​(k)=wL+kn​wT=0.35+k.\alpha^{*}(k)=\frac{w_{L}+k}{nw_{T}}=0.35+k.

Below this boundary the query remains socially beneficial but is privately dominated; above it, private and social incentives favor querying.


Figure 3: Private-share incentive isolation for GPT-5.6 Sol. A: The observed private-share threshold at which query rate reaches 50% (blue) closely follows the Holmström-derived prediction (red dashed) across all nine query costs; gray segments show the small prediction errors. B: Pooling the nine costs at equal distances from their predicted boundaries, the model never queries just below the boundary, mixes at private indifference, and always queries just above it. Each bar aggregates 405 decisions; whiskers are Wilson 95% confidence intervals. The full 67-cell sweep is reported in Appendix D.


Across all nine query costs, the empirical 50% query threshold tracks the predicted threshold with mean absolute error 0.013 and maximum error 0.020. Pooling across costs, query rate changes from 0.0%0.0\% just below the boundary to 68.9%68.9\% at indifference and 100.0%100.0\% just above it. Across the full 67-cell design, increasing cost from k=0.00k=0.00 to k=0.40k=0.40 reduces query rate by 26.726.7 points (95% bootstrap CI [−32.9,−20.9][-32.9,-20.9]), whereas increasing private share from αi=0.00\alpha_{i}=0.00 to αi=1.00\alpha_{i}=1.00 raises it by 100.0100.0 points (95% CI [100.0,100.0][100.0,100.0]). Payoff comprehension, private-action prediction, and format validity are all 100.0%100.0\%.


Together, the autonomous sweeps and incentive isolation support a scoped construct-validity claim: behavior responds to the implemented payoff contract, and the isolated focal decision follows the sufficient private margin in Equation 4. This validates the implemented private-versus-social incentive mechanism, not the stronger claim that every autonomous failure is uniquely moral hazard or that the experiment re-proves Holmström’s theorem. Full cells, boundary estimates, and matched contrasts appear in Appendix D.
